subject: science
title: KS3 / Year 7-9 Science — Ecosystems Reading
subtitle: Reading passages for KS3 ecosystems, food webs, biodiversity, human impacts and fieldwork.
description: A reading pack for KS3 biology ecosystems. Passages focus on ecosystem structure, feeding relationships, biodiversity, population changes, human impacts, conservation and ecological fieldwork.

data.sourcePassage: An ecosystem is made from all the living organisms in an area, the non-living conditions around them and the interactions between them. A pond, woodland, garden, hedgerow, rocky shore or school field can all be ecosystems. In a pond, the living parts include pondweed, algae, snails, tadpoles, fish, frogs, bacteria and fungi. The non-living parts include water, mud, rocks, oxygen, light and temperature. An ecosystem is not just a place. It includes the organisms, the physical conditions and the relationships that link them. Organisms are interdependent because they rely on each other for food, shelter, pollination, decomposition and population control.

questions.question: What three things make up an ecosystem?
questions.modelAnswer: Living organisms, non-living conditions and the interactions between them.

questions.question: Which of these could be a small ecosystem?
questions.modelAnswer: A rotting log can be a small ecosystem.

questions.question: Name two non-living parts of a pond ecosystem.
questions.modelAnswer: Water, mud, rocks, oxygen, light and temperature are possible answers.

questions.question: Why is an ecosystem more than just a place?
questions.modelAnswer: It includes organisms, physical conditions and the relationships between organisms and their environment.

questions.question: Give one example of interdependence from an ecosystem.
questions.modelAnswer: For example, bees depend on flowers for nectar and flowering plants may depend on bees for pollination.

data.sourceTitle: Food Chains, Food Webs and Energy
data.targetTitle: Food Chains, Food Webs and Energy
data.sourcePassage: A food chain shows one pathway of energy transfer through feeding. It begins with a producer, such as grass, algae or pondweed. Consumers get energy by eating other organisms. In the food chain grass -> rabbit -> fox, the arrow means energy moves from the grass to the rabbit and then from the rabbit to the fox. The arrow does not point to what gets eaten; it shows energy moving from food to feeder. Food webs are more realistic than food chains because most organisms eat more than one type of food and may be eaten by more than one predator. Decomposers such as bacteria, fungi and earthworms break down dead material and waste.

questions.question: What does the arrow in a food chain show?
questions.modelAnswer: The arrow shows the direction of energy transfer.
options: The organism that is least important

questions.question: What type of organism usually begins a food chain?
questions.modelAnswer: A producer usually begins a food chain.

questions.question: Explain why grass -> rabbit -> fox is in the correct order.
questions.modelAnswer: Grass is the producer, the rabbit eats the grass, and the fox eats the rabbit, so energy moves from grass to rabbit to fox.

questions.question: Why are food webs more realistic than food chains?
questions.modelAnswer: Most organisms have more than one food source and may be eaten by more than one predator, so many food chains are connected.

questions.question: Name two decomposers mentioned in the passage.
questions.modelAnswer: Bacteria, fungi and earthworms are decomposers.

data.sourcePassage: Biodiversity means the variety of living organisms in an area. It includes plants, animals, fungi, microorganisms and the variety of habitats. High biodiversity can make an ecosystem more stable and resilient. In a biodiverse food web, a predator may have several prey species. If one prey species decreases, the predator may be able to eat another. A habitat with many plant species may support more insects, birds and decomposers than a habitat with only one plant species. Low biodiversity can make ecosystems more vulnerable. For example, if a field contains only one crop species, a disease affecting that crop may damage the whole field.

questions.question: What does biodiversity mean?
questions.modelAnswer: Biodiversity is the variety of living organisms in an area.

questions.question: Which list best shows what biodiversity includes?
questions.modelAnswer: Biodiversity includes plants, animals, fungi, microorganisms and habitats.
options: Plants, animals, fungi, microorganisms and habitats

questions.question: Why can high biodiversity make an ecosystem more stable?
questions.modelAnswer: There may be more feeding relationships and alternative food sources, so the ecosystem may recover better after a change.

questions.question: Why might a field with only one crop species be vulnerable?
questions.modelAnswer: A disease affecting that crop could damage much of the field because there is little variety.

questions.question: Explain how plant biodiversity can affect animal biodiversity.
questions.modelAnswer: More plant species can provide more food and habitats for insects, birds and decomposers, so more animal species may be supported.

data.sourcePassage: Human activity can harm ecosystems through habitat destruction, pollution, pesticides, overfishing, hunting, climate change and introducing non-native species. Pesticides may directly reduce insect numbers. This can also indirectly affect insect-eating birds because they have less food. If pollinators such as bees decrease, some flowering plants may produce fewer seeds. Humans can also protect ecosystems. Conservation actions include creating nature reserves, planting hedgerows and wildflowers, reducing pollution, using sustainable fishing, building wildlife corridors and protecting pollinators. Conservation works best when the action matches the problem, such as reducing run-off to improve pond water quality.

questions.question: Name two human activities that can harm ecosystems.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include habitat destruction, pollution, pesticides, overfishing, hunting, climate change and introducing non-native species.

questions.question: Give one direct effect of pesticide use.
questions.modelAnswer: A direct effect is that insect numbers may decrease because pesticides kill insects.

questions.question: Give one indirect effect of pesticide use.
questions.modelAnswer: Insect-eating birds may decrease because they have less food, or plants may produce fewer seeds if pollinators decrease.

questions.question: Which action would most directly help pollinators?
questions.modelAnswer: Planting wildflowers and reducing pesticide use can help pollinators.
options: Planting wildflowers and reducing pesticide use

questions.question: Why should conservation actions match the problem?
questions.modelAnswer: Different problems affect ecosystems in different ways, so the most useful action targets the cause, such as reducing run-off when pond oxygen is affected by pollution.

data.sourcePassage: Ecologists collect evidence about organisms in habitats. In school fieldwork, students may compare plant biodiversity in a mown area and an unmown wildflower area using quadrats. A quadrat is placed at random positions, and students count the number of different plant species inside it. They repeat the method several times in each habitat and calculate a mean. The independent variable is the habitat type. The dependent variable is the number of plant species per quadrat. Control variables include quadrat size, number of samples and the counting method. Reliability can be improved by using more quadrats. Students should avoid damaging habitats and should handle living organisms gently.

questions.question: What piece of equipment is used to sample plants in a set area?
questions.modelAnswer: A quadrat is used to sample plants in a set area.

questions.question: In this investigation, what is the independent variable?
questions.modelAnswer: The independent variable is habitat type, such as mown area or unmown wildflower area.

questions.question: What is the dependent variable?
questions.modelAnswer: The dependent variable is the number of plant species per quadrat.

questions.question: How could students improve reliability?
questions.modelAnswer: They could use more quadrats, repeat the sampling and calculate a mean.

questions.question: Why is ethical care important in ecosystem fieldwork?
questions.modelAnswer: Fieldwork studies living things and habitats, so students should avoid unnecessary harm and return organisms to their habitats.
